DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%" -- The hotel is described as a 112-room hotel in the Context section, but the revenue estimate uses 124 rooms. With 112 rooms the same calculation gives 112 x 104 x 0.79 x £20 = about £184,000, not £204,000.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels" -- The only evidence is that occupancy rose from June to July after a June rate rise, but the document itself says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. The seasonal rise confounds the comparison; it cannot show demand is price-insensitive (let alone that the higher price helped).
3. [missing_consideration] at: "We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above." -- The document states that about 38% of Saturday-night bookings are wedding guests from the adjacent venue who stay only Saturday night. A two-night minimum would exclude or deter this group, but the revenue case assumes occupancy is maintained and never addresses the loss of these single-night Saturday bookings.

REVIEW:
# Review: Weekend Rate Restructure, Harbourside Hotel

**Overall:** The case for a weekend rate rise may well be sound. We're £20–35 below the competitive set, and Saturdays sell out often. But the three pillars of the author's argument don't hold up against the document's own data:
- The price-sensitivity "test" is a seasonal effect.
- The £204,000 is calculated on the wrong room count, and applies the increase to rooms that won't pay it.
- The two-night minimum conflicts with 38% of the Saturday business.

The £204k is a gross overstatement, not a floor.

## Major issues

### 1. The June-to-July "test" shows seasonality, not low price sensitivity
Occupancy rose from 81% in June to 89% in July. But the document itself says July and August are the strongest months, "driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays." The rest of Table 1 follows the same seasonal shape: 93% in August, then a fall to 72% by November. A rise after June would be expected at any price.

Supporting price insensitivity would need one of these:
- July 2025 compared with July 2024, when the rate was unchanged;
- pick-up and booking pace compared with the prior year;
- a comparison against the competitive set's occupancy over the same months.

Otherwise the claim that the higher rate "reinforced our positioning" has no support. And the author's statement that "everything points the same way" depends mainly on this one comparison.

### 2. The revenue calculation uses the wrong room count
Section 2 says the hotel has **112 rooms**, but section 5 uses **124**:
- 124 × 104 × 79% × £20 = **£203,757**, which is the stated figure.
- 112 × 104 × 79% × £20 = **£184,038**

That overstates the gain by about £20k before any other adjustment.

### 3. The increase applies only to BAR rooms, not every occupied room
The calculation assumes every occupied weekend room pays £20 more. But the document says contracted corporate and group rates will be honoured, and wedding blocks are **38% of Saturday bookings**. None of these pay BAR.

As an illustration only, if around 30% of weekend room nights are on group or contracted rates, the uplift falls to about **£130k**. Further deductions also apply:
- OTA commission, often 15–20%, on the share sold through those channels;
- VAT, if the figures are gross.

The paper should calculate the gain on actual BAR room nights by channel.

### 4. The two-night minimum works against the Saturday business
The paper says wedding guests "arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning," and they are 38% of Saturday bookings. A blanket two-night minimum on stays that include a Saturday would either:
- turn these guests away to competitors, possibly damaging the Quayside Hall relationship; or
- be waived for them, in which case it does nothing for 38% of Saturday demand.

Leisure guests who want one night will also go elsewhere. The hotel sold out on 31 Saturdays, so on the other **21** a minimum-stay rule mostly loses bookings rather than lengthening them.

So the minimum has a real downside, and the author's claim that leaving it unvalued makes £204k "a floor" is wrong. The usual practice is to apply minimum stays only on dates forecast to sell out, with explicit exemptions for group blocks.

### 5. "Assumes no occupancy change" isn't conservative
Holding occupancy at 2025 levels after a 14% rate rise is the *optimistic* case, given that the evidence for price insensitivity is seasonal (issue 1). The paper should instead show a break-even calculation. On BAR rooms, revenue per occupied room rises from £145 to £165. Occupancy can therefore fall by about **12% in relative terms**, roughly 79% to 69%, before room revenue is lower than today, before counting the minimum-stay effect. This shows real headroom, and it's a far stronger argument than an unsupported claim of price insensitivity.

## Other points

6. **The value-for-money score measures the current position.** The 8.4 was earned at £145, when we were the cheapest in the set. At £165 we would match the cheapest competitor, so the score is just as likely to fall. It isn't evidence that guests will absorb the rise.

7. **The monitoring trigger is in the wrong place and uses the wrong measure.**
   - **Reporting is monthly**, so a shortfall shows up only after a full month of bookings at the new rate. Weekly pick-up is tracked, so the trigger should run on that weekly pace.
   - **Occupancy alone won't reveal a problem.** Given the break-even calculation above, a five-point fall is still revenue-positive. RevPAR is the right metric.
   - **Friday and Saturday need tracking separately.** The minimum stay could raise Friday occupancy while Saturday falls, hiding the effect in a combined figure.
   - **The response is undefined.** "Review the rate" should say what happens next.

8. **The "protected" commitments are only those already contracted.** Future wedding blocks and group contracts aren't covered, and these are the bookings the minimum stay most affects.

9. **First-year revenue.** The change starts on 1 June, so "annual" means June to May. It also takes effect just ahead of the peak months, July and August, when demand is least sensitive to price. Early results may therefore look better than the rest of the year will.

## Suggested fixes

1. **Replace the June-to-July evidence** with a year-on-year or competitor-relative comparison, or drop the price-insensitivity claim and rely on the competitor gap and the break-even analysis.
2. **Recalculate the revenue** using 112 rooms and actual BAR room nights, net of commission, and add a break-even occupancy table.
3. **Redesign the minimum stay.** Apply it only on high-demand dates, exempt wedding and group blocks, and agree the approach with Quayside Hall.
4. **Make the monitoring weekly.** Track RevPAR separately for Friday and Saturday, and define what action follows a breach.
5. **Restate the recommendation** with a range, not "at least £204,000."

A rate rise toward the competitive set is probably the right decision. The proposal should rest on the figures that actually support it.
